1	// Package paths establishes which project harnaas is acting on and carries it
2	// in the request context.
3	//
4	// Every path a command touches resolves against the project root, never against
5	// the process working directory: `harnaas install` run from `src/api/` has to
6	// install into the same places as the same command run from the repository
7	// root, and `harnaas lint` has to report the same findings from either. Reading
8	// the working directory at a use site quietly makes the answer depend on where
9	// the user happened to stand.
10	//
11	// So the root is resolved once, at the entrypoint, and read from the context
12	// everywhere else. forbidigo bans os.Getwd across the repository with a message
13	// naming ProjectRoot(ctx) as the replacement; WithDiscoveredRoot below is the
14	// single sanctioned reader of the working directory, and it exists only to feed
15	// that carrier. Nothing here resolves a root a second time.
16	package paths
17	
18	import (
19		"context"
20		"fmt"
21		"os"
22		"path/filepath"
23	)
24	
25	// RepositoryMarker is the entry whose presence makes a directory the root of a
26	// repository. Git writes it as a directory in an ordinary clone and as a file in
27	// a worktree or a submodule, so the search below tests for existence and not for
28	// a directory — refusing to run inside a worktree would be an arbitrary
29	// restriction, not a safety property.
30	const RepositoryMarker = ".git"
31	
32	// ErrRootNotEstablished reports that the context never passed through
33	// WithDiscoveredRoot or WithProjectRoot. It is a wiring failure rather than
34	// anything the user did: some caller built a context by hand and gave it to a
35	// command. The message still reads as a diagnostic because an error that can
36	// reach a terminal must, and it names the fix a developer needs.
37	var ErrRootNotEstablished error = rootNotEstablishedError{}
38	
39	// rootNotEstablishedError carries ErrRootNotEstablished's message. It is a type
40	// rather than an errors.New value so the message can be a problem and a fix
41	// separated by a blank line, like every other diagnostic here, instead of the
42	// single unpunctuated clause a bare sentinel is held to.
43	type rootNotEstablishedError struct{}
44	
45	func (rootNotEstablishedError) Error() string {
46		return "no project root was established for this command\n\n" +
47			"Build the command's context with paths.WithDiscoveredRoot before executing it."
48	}
49	
50	// NoProjectRootError reports that Dir is not inside a repository, so there is no
51	// project for a command to act on.
52	//
53	// It is a type rather than a formatted string so a command can recognise the
54	// condition — `init` may want to say something about starting a repository
55	// where `lint` only wants to fail — without matching on message text.
56	type NoProjectRootError struct {
57		// Dir is the absolute directory the upward search started from. Naming it
58		// is most of the diagnostic: "not inside a repository" is puzzling until
59		// the user sees which directory harnaas was actually looking at.
60		Dir string
61	}
62	
63	// Error states the problem and the edit that fixes it, in that order, as every
64	// user-facing diagnostic does.
65	func (e *NoProjectRootError) Error() string {
66		return fmt.Sprintf(
67			"no project root found: %s is not inside a repository\n\n"+
68				"Run harnaas from inside your project's repository, or create one there with `git init`.",
69			e.Dir,
70		)
71	}
72	
73	// rootKey is the context key for the resolved root. An unexported struct type
74	// cannot collide with a key from any other package.
75	type rootKey struct{}
76	
77	// resolution is what the context carries: the root that was found, or the
78	// failure to find one.
79	//
80	// The failure travels rather than aborting at the entrypoint because most of
81	// what harnaas can do needs no project at all — `--version`, `--help`, an
82	// unknown-command diagnostic — and refusing to start outside a repository would
83	// break every one of them. A command that needs a root asks for one and gets the
84	// failure then, at the moment it is relevant.
85	type resolution struct {
86		root string
87		err  error
88	}
89	
90	// Resolve walks up from startDir and returns the first enclosing directory
91	// holding a RepositoryMarker, or a *NoProjectRootError if the walk reaches the
92	// filesystem root without finding one.
93	//
94	// The nearest enclosing repository wins, so a command run inside a submodule
95	// acts on the submodule. That is the same answer git itself gives, and a rule
96	// that agrees with git is one users already know.
97	func Resolve(startDir string) (string, error) {
98		dir, err := filepath.Abs(startDir)
99		if err != nil {
100			return "", fmt.Errorf("resolve %s to an absolute path: %w", startDir, err)
101		}
102	
103		for {
104			if _, err := os.Stat(filepath.Join(dir, RepositoryMarker)); err == nil {
105				return dir, nil
106			}
107	
108			parent := filepath.Dir(dir)
109			if parent == dir {
110				// filepath.Dir is its own fixed point at the filesystem root, and
111				// on Windows at a volume root too, so this is the end of the walk
112				// on every platform without special-casing either.
113				return "", &NoProjectRootError{Dir: filepath.Clean(startDir)}
114			}
115			dir = parent
116		}
117	}
118	
119	// WithProjectRoot returns a context carrying root as the project root, for a
120	// caller that already knows it — a test over a scratch project, or a future
121	// command that resolves a project some other way.
122	func WithProjectRoot(ctx context.Context, root string) context.Context {
123		return context.WithValue(ctx, rootKey{}, resolution{root: root})
124	}
125	
126	// WithDiscoveredRoot resolves the project root from the process working
127	// directory and returns a context carrying either the root or the failure.
128	//
129	// This is the one place in harnaas that reads the working directory. It runs
130	// once, at the entrypoint, before any command executes; every other site calls
131	// ProjectRoot. Neither failure — an unreadable working directory or a directory
132	// outside any repository — is reported here, because at this point nobody knows
133	// yet whether the command about to run needs a project.
134	func WithDiscoveredRoot(ctx context.Context) context.Context {
135		//nolint:forbidigo // The ban names ProjectRoot(ctx) as the replacement; this is the function that fills it, and the only sanctioned reader of the working directory.
136		wd, err := os.Getwd()
137		if err != nil {
138			return context.WithValue(ctx, rootKey{}, resolution{
139				err: fmt.Errorf("determine the working directory to resolve the project root from: %w", err),
140			})
141		}
142	
143		root, err := Resolve(wd)
144		return context.WithValue(ctx, rootKey{}, resolution{root: root, err: err})
145	}
146	
147	// ProjectRoot returns the project root carried by ctx.
148	//
149	// This is the replacement forbidigo's message names, and the only supported way
150	// to learn where the project is. A command that calls it is declaring that it
151	// needs a project, which is why the discovery failure surfaces here rather than
152	// at the entrypoint.
153	func ProjectRoot(ctx context.Context) (string, error) {
154		res, ok := ctx.Value(rootKey{}).(resolution)
155		if !ok {
156			return "", ErrRootNotEstablished
157		}
158		if res.err != nil {
159			return "", res.err
160		}
161		return res.root, nil
162	}

# harnaas

A CLI that manages a project's AI-harness configuration as a declared, versioned dependency. A team
states which assets it wants in a manifest; `harnaas install` fetches them and places them where each
harness expects; `harnaas lint` verifies that what is installed still matches what was declared.

## Language

### The things being managed

**Harness**:
An AI coding tool that reads its configuration from files in a project or a user home — Claude Code,
Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI.
_Avoid_: agent, editor, client, host, IDE

**Asset**:
A single unit of harness configuration that harnaas installs — one skill, rule, instruction, command
or persona.
_Avoid_: artifact, resource, plugin, extension, capability

=== 60-100 ===
**Source**:
Where an asset's content comes from — a path within a GitHub repository at some ref, or a path under
the project's `.harnaas` directory.

**Scope**:
Which root an asset installs beneath — `project` for the repository's own harness directory, `user`
for the harness's per-user home.

**Managed**:
Describes a destination recorded in the lockfile. harnaas may update or remove a managed destination,
because it put it there.

**Unmanaged**:
Describes a destination that exists on disk but is not recorded in the lockfile. harnaas never
overwrites or deletes one, on any flag.

**Drift**:
The condition of a managed destination whose content no longer matches what was installed — somebody
edited it outside harnaas.

**Managed block**:
A marker-delimited region harnaas owns inside a file the team also writes. Everything outside it is
preserved untouched. Used where harnaas must contribute to a file it cannot own outright — the
project's memory file and its version-control ignore file.

**Shared target**:
A destination more than one harness reads, so a single write serves several of them. Contrast with a
per-harness target, which only its own harness reads.

**Emulated**:
Describes an asset installed through a different type's surface because its own is absent on that
harness — a command delivered as a skill that the model will not invoke on its own. Reported as its
own outcome, never as plain success.

**Support tier**:
How current a harness surface is, which decides whether harnaas will write to it: live surfaces are
written, removed ones are refused, and gated or deprecated ones are written with a note.

**Convergence**:
Install bringing the installed set into agreement with the manifest, including removing assets that
are no longer declared.

1	// Package palette is the single source of truth for the colours harnaas puts on
2	// a terminal.
3	//
4	// Every colour here is a base16 slot — an ANSI number from 0 to 15 — and never
5	// a hex value or a 256-colour code. A slot is a request the terminal answers
6	// with its own theme, so harnaas's output inherits whatever the user already
7	// chose. A hex value overrides that choice, and the override is only ever right
8	// on the machine it was picked on: the shade of grey that reads as "secondary"
9	// against a dark background is invisible against a light one.
10	//
11	// The constants are plain strings rather than any styling library's colour
12	// type, which is what keeps this package dependency-free and importable from
13	// anywhere without an import cycle. A caller wraps as its own renderer requires.
14	//
15	// Reach for the bright slots (8–15) and for the renderer's faint attribute to
16	// build hierarchy. Adding a colour outside this file is how a CLI ends up with
17	// four different greys, none of which agree.
18	package palette
19	
20	// The base16 slots, named after the ANSI colour each number selects.
21	const (
22		Black         = "0"
23		Red           = "1"
24		Green         = "2"
25		Yellow        = "3"
26		Blue          = "4"
27		Magenta       = "5"
28		Cyan          = "6"
29		White         = "7"
30		BrightBlack   = "8"
31		BrightRed     = "9"
32		BrightGreen   = "10"
33		BrightYellow  = "11"
34		BrightBlue    = "12"
35		BrightMagenta = "13"
36		BrightCyan    = "14"
37		BrightWhite   = "15"
38	)
39	
40	// The semantic aliases. Style against these, and keep the raw slot names for
41	// the rare case where a colour carries no meaning at all — a slot name in a
42	// style declaration says what the colour is, where an alias says why it is
43	// there, and only the second survives a change of palette.
44	//
45	// There is deliberately no alias for body text, and adding one is the mistake
46	// this comment exists to prevent. Body text is left unstyled so it renders in
47	// the terminal's own default foreground, which inverts with the background.
48	// Pinning it to White would make every line of harnaas's output invisible on a
49	// light terminal, and pinning it to Black would do the same on a dark one.
50	// Unstyled is the only setting that is correct on both.
51	const (
52		// Accent marks the one thing on screen the user is meant to look at first.
53		Accent = Magenta
54		// Accent2 frames detail that belongs to the accented thing without
55		// competing with it.
56		Accent2 = BrightMagenta
57		// Muted is the single colour for secondary text, hints and borders. One
58		// muted slot rather than a range of greys is what keeps de-emphasis
59		// reading as one level instead of four.
60		Muted = BrightBlack
61		// Success, Error, Warning and Info carry outcome. These four map onto the
62		// colours a terminal user already reads as good, bad, careful and
63		// incidental, so they are not re-pointed to fit a brand.
64		Success = Green
65		Error   = Red
66		Warning = Yellow
67		Info    = Cyan
68	)

# harnaas

A Go CLI that manages a project's AI-harness assets as a declared, versioned dependency:
`harnaas.json` declares them, `harnaas install` places them, `harnaas lint` verifies them.

Two documents this file deliberately does not duplicate:

- **[CONTEXT.md](CONTEXT.md)** — the canonical vocabulary. *Harness*, *asset*, *skill*, *rule*,
  *instruction*, *command*, *persona*, *manifest*, *lockfile*, *managed*, *drift*, *finding*. Use
  these words and avoid the listed alternatives, in code, in output and in commit messages. Note in
  particular that the *manifest* is `harnaas.json` and the *lockfile* is `harnaas.lock.json` — the
  entire.io CLI this architecture is imported from uses "manifest" for the lockfile's role. Do not
  "correct" harnaas to match it.
- **[docs/adr/](docs/adr/)** — the load-bearing product decisions. Cite an ADR rather than
  re-arguing it; if you need to contradict one, write a new ADR.

## Architecture

The architecture is imported wholesale from the entire.io CLI (`github.com/entireio/cli`) rather
than designed fresh. The rules below are the imported ones plus harnaas's deliberate divergences.

### Layout

- `cmd/harnaas/` — the process entrypoint, and nothing else.
- `cmd/harnaas/cli/` — the bulk of the code, in one flat package. Command files are named
  `<noun>_group.go` for a group root and `<noun>_<verb>.go` for a leaf command.
- `internal/` — reserved for genuinely cross-binary code.
- A subpackage is extracted **only** to break a Go import cycle. That is the whole extraction
  trigger. There is no `domain` / `usecase` / `adapter` layering, and adding one is not an
  improvement — importing half an architecture buys the costs of both.

### Stack

cobra + pflag for the command tree, the Charm v2 stack on the `charm.land` module domain for
interactive surfaces, testify with gotestsum for tests. **No configuration library**: configuration
is `encoding/json` plus cobra flags plus environment variables, with precedence documented at each
read site.

mise is the single toolchain and task entry point (`mise run check` = fmt, then lint, then test).
Keep the Go version in `mise.toml` and the `go` directive in `go.mod` identical.

### The root command carries no persistent flags

A flag that applies to some commands is registered locally on each command that honours it —
`--json` included. A persistent `--json` would be accepted and silently ignored by every
side-effecting verb, and cobra cannot hide a persistent flag from a subset of children. Accepting a
flag and honouring it must be the same act.

### The entrypoint is the only component that prints an error or picks an exit code

Cobra's error and usage printing is silenced globally. The entrypoint switches on the returned
error and decides what to print and how to exit. A command that has already printed a friendly
explanation returns an error marked as already-printed — still unwrappable, so callers can inspect
the cause. Everything else is returned raw. Never print an error and also return it unmarked.

Exit codes: `0` success, `1` runtime failure, `2` **reserved** for a `lint` run that completed and
found error-severity findings, `128`+signum for signals. No command other than `lint` may exit `2`.

### Signals are re-raised, not swallowed

The first interrupt cancels the root context and prints a force-quit notice; a second terminates
immediately. On termination the process re-raises the original signal to itself rather than calling
a plain exit, falling back to `128`+signum only where re-raising is unsupported. A shell aborts a
`while true; do …; done` loop only when the child is *killed by* the signal — a plain exit with
status 130 is an ordinary exit, and the user's Ctrl-C never escapes the loop.

### The project root travels in `context.Context`

Resolved once from the enclosing repository and carried in the request context. Reading the process
working directory is banned by `forbidigo`, whose message names the replacement. There is no global
`-C` flag.

### Decoding strictness follows who writes the file

Committed, human-edited files decode **strictly** — an unknown field is nearly always a typo.
Machine-rewritten files decode **leniently** — a newer binary introduces fields an older binary
would otherwise reject, bricking the file with no fix available to the user who hits it. That test,
not the filename, is why `harnaas.json` is strict and `harnaas.lock.json` is lenient.

### harnaas never writes the manifest, and every remedy is an edit

Apart from `init` creating it once, no command writes, reformats or normalizes `harnaas.json`. This
is why there is no `add`, `remove` or `update` command. The manifest is what a team reviews; a tool
that rewrites it makes its diffs untrustworthy. Phrase every remedy as the exact edit that fixes
it, not as a fix command.

### Output streams and logging

User-facing text goes to `cmd.OutOrStdout()`; advisory, progress and warning text to
`cmd.ErrOrStderr()`. Under `--json` the document is the only thing on stdout. Cobra's `Print*`
helpers write to stderr and are banned by `forbidigo`.

Diagnostics go to a log file through `log/slog`, never to the terminal — and never to a stream as a
fallback either: where the file cannot be opened, records are discarded, because a fallback that
turns a disk problem into a corrupted `--json` document is worse than no logging. The file lives
under the user's cache directory (`HARNAAS_LOG_FILE` overrides it), not under the project, so no
command leaves a log behind in a team's working tree. **Identifiers, paths,
durations, counts and outcomes may be logged. File contents, prompt or memory text, captured output
and credentials may not.** The files harnaas handles are a team's instructions and rules — exactly
the content nobody expects to find copied into a log they did not know existed.

### Non-interactive completeness

Every workflow is completable without a terminal, and no information is reachable only through a
prompt, picker or full-screen interface. The primary consumers are CI jobs and coding agents,
neither of which has a terminal. Prompts render through an accessible-mode wrapper, and colour
comes from the terminal's own base palette with body text left unstyled.

Whether a prompt may be shown is answered from the command's own streams plus the environment, never
by probing a controlling terminal: a coding agent hands its subprocess a real terminal nobody is
watching, and `harnaas init > out.txt` has one attached and still must not prompt. The decision is
biased towards "no", because a flag-driven path always exists while a prompt shown to something that
cannot answer does not degrade — it hangs.

A cancelled prompt is not a "no". Declining and walking away are different acts, and a command that
folds them together does the declined thing to a user who asked for nothing at all.

### Diagnostics have a shape

Every user-facing diagnostic is `{problem, fix}`: what is wrong, and the exact edit or command that
resolves it. Validation accumulates every violation into one aggregate error, ordered
deterministically, rather than stopping at the first.

### Writes are atomic

Files are staged in the destination directory, synced, renamed into place, and the staging file is
removed on both success and failure. A failed write leaves the previous file intact.

### Static analysis encodes the rules

golangci-lint runs the standard set plus the extended list in `.golangci.yaml`. `forbidigo` turns
"go through the abstraction" into a build failure whose message names the replacement. `nolintlint`
requires every suppression to name a specific linter and give a reason, so widening a rule is
visible in review. Where a rule must survive a suppression, it is also asserted by an AST test over
non-test sources.

## Deliberately not here

Telemetry, authentication, self-update and a plugin system. The source CLI has all four; none pays
off across three commands, and each adds a dependency and a privacy surface.
